$comment: England & Wales, Employment Law, unfair dismissal (ordinary and automatic/whistleblowing). Promoted from real verification work already done this session in matters/M1-KESTREL/authorities/authorities.json (a live stress-test matter workspace) and examples/employment-tribunal-full-chambers/opposition/opposition_case.md, not fresh research - both were independently fetched/cross-checked at the time they were first verified, this is a reformat into the reusable Authority Graph, not a re-verification. See each entry's own verification_note for its original source trail. One deliberately excluded: matters/M1-KESTREL's AUTH-007 (Raison v DF Capital Bank Ltd) was logged UNVERIFIED there and never relied upon - not promoted here for that reason, a genuine research lead for a future session, not a verified authority.
verification_method: Mixed - see each entry. Case law mostly VERIFIED_SECONDARY_SOURCE (BAILII blocked direct fetch with HTTP 403 throughout, corroborated instead via 2-4 independent secondary sources per case per docs/OPERATING_RULES.md's verification hierarchy). The two statutory provisions were VERIFIED_PRIMARY_SOURCE, fetched directly from legislation.gov.uk.

authorities.name: British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell
authorities.date_note: Year only - exact day/month not independently pinpointed this session.
authorities.proposition: For ordinary unfair dismissal (ERA 1996 s.98), a dismissal for misconduct is fair where the employer genuinely believed the employee was guilty of the misconduct, had reasonable grounds for that belief, and had carried out as much investigation as was reasonable in the circumstances - not proof to a criminal standard.
authorities.verification_note: BAILII/ICLR text not located this session. Cross-checked via Croner-i, Personnel Today, and Fieldfisher - three independent, consistent sources.

authorities.name: Iceland Frozen Foods Ltd v Jones
authorities.proposition: A tribunal reviewing the fairness of a dismissal must not substitute its own view of the right course of action for the employer's; the question is only whether the decision to dismiss fell within the 'band of reasonable responses' a reasonable employer might have adopted.
authorities.verification_note: Cross-checked via Croner-i, Wikipedia, and doihaveacase.co.uk - three independent, consistent sources, including the date/citation discrepancy explained (judgment 29 July 1982, reported [1983] ICR 17 the following year).

authorities.name: Polkey v A E Dayton Services Ltd
authorities.date_note: Year only - exact day/month not independently pinpointed this session.
authorities.proposition: A dismissal can be procedurally unfair even where the employee might still have been fairly dismissed had a correct procedure been followed - but the compensatory award may then be reduced, including to nil, by the tribunal's assessed percentage chance that dismissal would have occurred anyway even with a fair procedure.
authorities.verification_note: Cross-checked via Wikipedia, Employment Law UK, and Personnel Today reporting - three independent, consistent sources. Repeatedly relied on across an earlier version of this matter's own moot record without ever being logged with a verification trail, corrected when this authority was actually verified.

authorities.name: Kuzel v Roche Products Ltd
authorities.proposition: In an ERA 1996 s.103A automatic unfair dismissal claim, the claimant must produce some evidence supporting the case that the protected disclosure was the reason for dismissal, but the legal burden never shifts to the claimant to prove that reason - it remains on the employer to show the reason (or principal reason) for dismissal, and if the employer's asserted reason is rejected, the tribunal must consider whether the true reason was the one alleged by the claimant.
authorities.verification_note: BAILII URL located via search but not fetched this session (same access restriction affecting BAILII throughout this matter's record). Corroborated via Croner, Practical Law, and swarb.co.uk secondary summaries.

authorities.name: Beatt v Croydon Health Services NHS Trust
authorities.proposition: Where the making of a disclosure is the principal reason for dismissal, whether the disclosure was in fact protected (reasonable belief, public interest) is a question for the tribunal to determine objectively - the employer's own belief that the disclosure was not protected, or was not made in good faith, is irrelevant to s.103A liability.
authorities.verification_note: BAILII URL located via search but not fetched this session. Corroborated via a 12 King's Bench Walk chambers note, Employment Cases Update, Croner-i, and Bird & Bird commentary.

authorities.name: Chesterton Global Ltd v Nurmohamed
authorities.date_note: Year only - exact day/month not independently pinpointed this session.
authorities.proposition: The 'public interest' test in ERA 1996 s.43B(1) (as amended by ERRA 2013 s.17, see AUTH-EW-EMPL-009) turns on whether the worker's belief that the disclosure was made in the public interest was itself objectively reasonable - a disclosure can still qualify even where it also serves the discloser's own interest, provided a section of the public beyond the discloser is also affected.
authorities.verification_note: BAILII direct fetch attempted this session at bailii.org/ew/cases/EWCA/Civ/2017/979.html and returned HTTP 403. Cross-checked via Croner-i, CMS Law-Now, Devereux Chambers, and Employment Cases Update reporting - four independent, consistent sources.

authorities.name: NHS Manchester v Fecitt and others
authorities.date_note: Approximate (2011-10-19 per secondary sources) - not independently pinpointed against BAILII's own date stamp this session.
authorities.proposition: For ERA 1996 s.47B whistleblowing detriment, causation is satisfied where the protected disclosure materially influenced (more than trivially) the employer's treatment of the worker - the stricter 'in no sense whatsoever' EU-discrimination-derived test does not apply. This causation test remains good law. A separate holding in this same case (no vicarious liability under s.47B for a co-worker's detriment absent a separate legal wrong by that co-worker) was legislatively superseded with effect from 25 June 2013 - see AUTH-EW-EMPL-008 and the QUALIFIES edge below.
authorities.verification_note: Direct BAILII fetch blocked by HTTP 403 this session; existence and holding corroborated via Employment Cases Update, Croner-i, CMS Law-Now, and Reed Smith commentary - independent-source corroboration, not a primary-source read.

authorities.name: Employment Rights Act 1996, s.47B(1A)-(1E) (inserted by Enterprise and Regulatory Reform Act 2013, s.19)
authorities.date_note: Date the amending provision came into force, not the date of the amending Act's Royal Assent.
authorities.proposition: Gives a worker a direct right of action against a co-worker or agent who subjects them to a s.47B whistleblowing detriment, treats that act as also done by the employer (vicarious liability), and gives the employer an 'all reasonable steps' defence to that vicarious liability - superseding NHS Manchester v Fecitt's earlier holding that there was no such vicarious liability for a co-worker's unconnected act.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched directly from legislation.gov.uk's in-force text and cross-checked against the enacting provision at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2013/24/section/19/enacted.

authorities.name: Enterprise and Regulatory Reform Act 2013, s.17 (public-interest amendment to ERA 1996 s.43B(1))
authorities.date_note: Year only - not independently fetched against legislation.gov.uk's enacted text this session, one tier below the live-legislation checks used for AUTH-EW-EMPL-008.
authorities.proposition: Inserted the requirement that a worker hold a reasonable belief the disclosure is made 'in the public interest', reversing Parkins v Sodexho Ltd [2002] IRLR 109, which had allowed a complaint about the discloser's own contract of employment alone to qualify. Enacted so that a complaint of a purely personal nature, with no wider public interest implications, no longer qualifies as a protected disclosure.
authorities.verification_note: Cross-checked via Lexology, No5 Barristers' Chambers, and Thomas Mansfield Employment Law commentary - three independent, consistent sources. Named explicitly as one tier below a live-legislation.gov.uk check, not overstated as equally strong.

edges.verified_via: ERA 1996 s.47B(1A)-(1E) (in force 2013-06-25) creates a co-worker vicarious-liability route Fecitt (2011) had held did not exist - the causation-test holding in Fecitt is unaffected and remains FOLLOWED; only the co-worker/vicarious-liability point is superseded, for any detriment falling after 25 June 2013.

Chesterton Global Ltd v Nurmohamed [2017] EWCA Civ 979 is the leading authority applying and clarifying the public-interest test ERRA 2013 s.17 created - the statute sets the requirement, Chesterton supplies the objective-reasonableness test for satisfying it.

Beatt v Croydon Health Services NHS Trust [2017] EWCA Civ 401 applies Kuzel's burden-of-proof framework, adding that whether a disclosure was in fact protected is assessed objectively by the tribunal, not by reference to the employer's own belief.

what_this_is_not: Nine verified nodes and three edges covering ordinary unfair dismissal reasonableness (Burchell, Iceland Frozen Foods), procedural fairness and remedy (Polkey), and automatic unfair dismissal/whistleblowing detriment (Kuzel, Beatt, Chesterton, Fecitt, and the two statutory provisions correcting/extending it). Does not cover redundancy, TUPE, discrimination beyond whistleblowing-adjacent detriment (see employment-disability-discrimination.json for that), or any procedural/tribunal-rules content - those remain unbuilt.
